transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Ms. Osei, thank you for meeting with me. I need to discuss the timeline of your care from yesterday and be honest about a mistake that happened.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I've been waiting for this. I know how the triage process works, and I know that my symptoms weren't handled according to the standard of care.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: You are correct. When you arrived, the triage nurse categorized you as low-acuity, meaning your symptoms weren't flagged as an emergency. Because of that, the imaging and the neurology consult were delayed. This delay meant that by the time we identified the stroke, the thrombolysis window—the timeframe where we can give the clot-busting medication—had already closed.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: The window. I know exactly what that window is. I'm a nurse practitioner, for god's sake. I sat in that waiting room for three hours watching people who arrived after me go back first.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I am very sorry. Our team failed to recognize the urgency of your presentation, and we are responsible for that delay.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: This isn't just a mistake. This is a systemic failure. I might have full mobility in my arm right now, but what about the long-term? What has this delay actually cost me in terms of my prognosis?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It is incredibly frightening to think about the permanency of these things.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Frightening? It's devastating. I could be looking at a permanent deficit because someone didn't follow a basic stroke screen. I can't even wrap my head around how this happens in a tertiary center.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can see you're really upset, and I know this is an overwhelming realization.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I'm not just upset. I'm terrified. I have a practice to run. I have a life. If I can't function, everything changes.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand that's a lot to process. But, I should mention that we need to move toward the next steps for your recovery.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Wait, you're just moving on? I just told you I'm scared and you're jumping to the next step?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I just mean we have a clear path forward. First, I have already scheduled a follow-up with the Chief of Neurology for tomorrow at 10 AM to review your specific imaging and determine the exact extent of the infarct. Second, we are starting you on a high-intensity rehabilitation protocol starting tomorrow morning at 8 AM. You'll be working with a physical therapist twice a day.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: And what about the "why"? Who is being held accountable?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I have already filed a formal incident report. The department head is conducting a root-cause analysis to determine why the triage screen failed in your case so we can implement a mandatory double-check system for any patient presenting with focal neurological deficits. This will prevent this from happening to someone else.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I hope so. I really hope so.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I will be your main point of contact. I'll check in with you every morning at 9 AM to review your therapy progress and answer any questions. I'll also provide you with a written copy of the incident report number for your own records by this evening. Do you feel those steps address the immediate concerns?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: It's a start. I just can't believe I'm the one in the bed this time.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I know. We'll take it one step at a time.

H.justification: The resident uses rushing language ('we need to move toward the next steps') while the patient is expressing fear.

E.justification: The error is named explicitly and early, but there are no comprehension checks performed throughout the transcript.

A.justification: The resident uses direct apology language ('I am very sorry') and explicitly states the team is responsible without deflection.

R.justification: The resident names specific emotions ('frightening', 'upset', 'overwhelming') and engages with the patient's distress.

T.justification: The resident provides specific next steps with timelines and addresses prevention, but does not name a specific role for the patient in the plan.
